text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The war of words between Prime Minister Goran Persson and Sweden's business leaders continues with head of the Business Association Bert-Olof Svanholm saying the minority Social Democrat government is now turning to "ecological fundamentalist policies." The battle started with a letter in a weekend newspaper signed by 101 business leaders opposing the phase out of the nuclear industry and criticising Persson for not listening to industry. Persson said he will personally contact several of the business leaders who signed the letter.

- The head of fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz Stefan Persson and his family are the richest on the Stockholm bourse. Last year H&M's shares rose over 150 percent and at the year's end Persson's shares were worth 17 billion crowns. The Wallenberg family's investment vehicle, Investor AB, was the biggest shareowner on the bourse with its holdings worth 73.1 billion crowns.

- The central bank, the Riksbank, was still seen to be on line with its goal for inflation of 1-3 percent a year, according to a survey of inflation expectations commissioned by the bank. Industry players expected inflation in five years time to be 2.0 percent and wage increases 2.9 percent. In one year's time inflation was seen at 1.5 percent and in two years 1.7 percent.

- Unions and employers are close to reaching an agreement about new wage deal rules. Blue collar umbrella union organisation LO is expected to propose that unions will have influence over each others' wage deals, which will prevent some unions getting higher wage increases than others.

- New products, among them glaucoma treatment drug Xalatan, helped lift drugs company Pharmacia & Upjohn's fourth quarter sales last year. In 1997, the company will focus on new product launches, which will be funded by some of the expected synergies from the merger between Pharmacia AB of Sweden and Upjohn Co of the U.S. into Pharmacia & Upjohn in 1995.

- The Centre Party, which closely cooperates with Sweden's minority Social Democrats government, aims to get more influence on the government's spring budget proposal by presenting its own programme, worth billions of crowns, to fight unemployment next week. In two weeks, the party and the government will probably start talks about the budget proposal.

- The Swedish system of imposing stiff penalties for tax law infractions with few if any avenues for appeal could be overturned if tested by the European Court. Penalites of up to 40 percent of the tax amount due can be imposed by local tax authoriites who in effect act like judge and jury.

- Swedish telephone operator Telia with several local partners is prepared to invest a minimum of seven billion crowns in Brazil to launch a mobile telephone network. The deadline on bids on licences to operate private networks in 10 regions of Brazil is April 7. The cost of entering the Brazilian market is high with the 10 concessions together carrying a pricetag of at least 25 billion crowns.
- Bo Andersson, a former executive of Sweden's Saab Auto, has been appointed as a new vice president of General Motors Europe, responsible for purchasing.

- Swedish/U.S. drugs group Pharmacia & Upjohn reported that sales grew 7.5 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 to $1.9 billion. Chief executive Jan Ekberg said he was satisfied with his company's fourth quarter earnings but said margin improvement were not up to expectations and there were many challenges ahead.
